needs: A laptop and a webcam, free hand-tracking software (MediaPipe), and time to collect videos. No special hardware. A contact in the deaf community or an ISL course would help a lot.
novelty: Very little ISL video data or software exists, so even a working recognizer for a few dozen everyday signs would be new. You could also test a cheap trick from the papers you starred: instead of feeding the whole video to a large AI model, first find the hands and face, then let a small model read only those points over time.
problem: Deaf people in Israel often have no interpreter at a clinic, a bank or a government office. Apps that turn signing into text exist for American and Chinese Sign Language, but almost nothing works for Israeli Sign Language (ISL).
related: SignVLA: Real-Time Sign Language-Guided Robotic Manipulation
Attention-Steered Vision-Language Models for Sign Language Translation
A vision-based sign language recognition and voice conversion system for inclusive communication
scope: Weeks 1–3: record or collect short videos of 30–50 common ISL signs (from volunteers or the Israeli deaf community's online dictionaries) and track hand points automatically. Weeks 4–8: train a small sequence model to recognize single signs, and test it on signers it never saw. Weeks 9–12: a live webcam demo that shows the recognized sign as text or speech, plus a short evaluation of what fails (lighting, fast signing, different hands).
title: A sign-language reader for Israeli Sign Language
